title: Exactly Twenty Terms
statement:
A repunit is a positive integer whose decimal digits are all equal to $1$, so the repunits are $1, 11, 111, \dots$.

How many positive integers less than $10^4$ can be written as a sum of exactly $20$ repunits, where the same repunit may be used more than once and the order of the terms does not matter?
hints: Multiply a repunit by $9$ and add $1$. What number do you get? Now see what happens to a sum $N$ of $20$ repunits when you form $9N + 20$.

Since $9R_k + 1 = 10^k$ for the repunit $R_k$ with $k$ digits, the number $Q = \frac{9N+20}{10}$ is a sum of exactly $20$ powers of ten, with exponents at least $0$. Use digit sums to decide which $Q$ can occur: replacing ten copies of a power of ten by the next power is a carry, and it lowers the number of terms by $9$.

With $Q = \frac{9N+20}{10}$, the valid values of $N$ correspond to the integers $Q$ with $20 \le Q \le 9001$ whose digit sum is $2$, $11$ or $20$. Stars and bars with inclusion-exclusion shows that the strings of $4$ digits with these digit sums number $10$, $348$ and $633$ respectively. It remains to discard the strings whose value lies outside the range.
solution: Let $R_k$ be the repunit with $k$ digits, so that $9R_k + 1 = 10^k$. If $N = R_{k_1} + \dots + R_{k_{20}}$, then $$9N + 20 = 10^{k_1} + \dots + 10^{k_{20}}.$$ Every $k_i$ is at least $1$, so $Q = \frac{9N+20}{10}$ is an integer, and it is a sum of exactly $20$ powers of ten with exponents at least $0$. Conversely, if $Q = 10^{e_1} + \dots + 10^{e_{20}}$ with each $e_i \ge 0$, then $N = R_{e_1+1} + \dots + R_{e_{20}+1}$ is a sum of $20$ repunits with $9N + 20 = 10Q$. Since $N$ and $Q$ determine each other, it suffices to count the possible values of $Q$. Also, $N \le 9999$ holds exactly when $10Q \le 90011$, that is, when $Q \le 9001$. Let $s(Q)$ be the digit sum of $Q$. We claim that $Q$ is a sum of exactly $20$ powers of ten if and only if $s(Q) \in \{2, 11, 20\}$ and $Q \ge 20$. Suppose first that $Q$ is such a sum. Each term is at least $1$, so $Q \ge 20$. While some power appears at least ten times, replace ten copies of it by one copy of the next power. This keeps the value and lowers the number of terms by $9$, so the process stops. At the end each power appears at most nine times, which is the decimal expansion of $Q$, with $s(Q)$ terms. Hence $s(Q) = 20 - 9t$ for some integer $t \ge 0$, and since $s(Q) > 0$ we get $s(Q) \in \{2, 11, 20\}$. Suppose instead that $s(Q) \in \{2, 11, 20\}$ and $Q \ge 20$. The decimal expansion writes $Q$ as a sum of $s(Q)$ powers of ten. If there are fewer than $20$ terms, they cannot all equal $1$, because their sum is at least $20$. So some term is at least $10$, and we replace it by ten copies of the next lower power, which adds $9$ terms. Repeating this reaches exactly $20$ terms, since $s(Q) \equiv 20 \pmod 9$ and $s(Q) \le 20$. So we must count the integers $Q$ with $20 \le Q \le 9001$ and $s(Q) \in \{2, 11, 20\}$. Write each integer from $0$ to $9999$ as a string of $4$ digits. By stars and bars, with inclusion-exclusion to remove digits of at least $10$, the number of strings with each digit sum is as follows. Digit sum $2$ gives $\binom{5}{3} = 10$. Digit sum $11$ gives $\binom{14}{3} - 4\binom{4}{3} = 348$. Digit sum $20$ gives $\binom{23}{3} - 4\binom{13}{3} + 6\binom{3}{3} = 633$. The total is $991$. Next we remove the values above $9001$. These have first digit $9$, and the other three digits form a number at least $2$. Digit sum $2$ is impossible here. Digit sum $11$ needs the last three digits to sum to $2$, giving $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ strings. Digit sum $20$ needs them to sum to $11$, giving $\binom{13}{2} - 3\binom{3}{2} = 69$ strings. All of these strings represent a three-digit part at least $2$, because the parts $000$ and $001$ have digit sums $0$ and $1$. So $75$ values are removed. Finally we remove the values below $20$. Among these, only $Q = 2$ and $Q = 11$ have an allowed digit sum, since numbers below $20$ have digit sum at most $10$ and only these two have digit sum $2$. The count is $991 - 75 - 2 = 914$, so the answer is $914$. Why this works. digit-sum-mod-9, variable-substitution: the substitution turns repunits into powers of ten, where each carry changes the number of terms by $9$, so the digit sum modulo $9$ decides which values are reachable.
